questions.question_text: A listed IT company is majority owned by a founding trust holding about 70% equity, while day-to-day operations are run entirely by non-family professional executives. Which quadrant of the ownership-management matrix best fits this company?

options.A: High family ownership with family management
options.B: Low family ownership with professional management
options.C: High family ownership with professional management
options.D: Low family ownership with family management

questions.explanation: A trust owning ~70% (like Tata Trusts in TCS) with fully professional management is high family ownership with professional management.

questions.question_text: Under which leadership condition do family-owned firms typically exhibit the strongest financial performance relative to non-family firms?

options.A: When a professional outside manager is hired to lead the corporation
options.B: When the founding family retains ownership but avoids holding active board seats
options.C: When institutional investors acquire the majority of voting control rights
options.D: When a family member serves as CEO instead of an outside professional

questions.explanation: Research cited in the module found family firms performed even better when a family member was CEO.

questions.question_text: How does the principle of shareholder value maximisation differ in meaning between a typical non-family business and a family business?

options.A: In a family business the shareholder is the family, so it becomes family value
options.B: Family businesses reject shareholder value maximisation entirely
options.C: Non-family businesses maximise employee value instead of shareholder value
options.D: Family businesses only maximise value for minority shareholders

questions.explanation: In a family business the shareholder is the family, so shareholder value maximisation becomes family value maximisation.

questions.question_text: In the four-quadrant framework of family business goals, which combination describes growth of the firm and improvements in firm performance?

options.A: Family-oriented economic goals
options.B: Non-family oriented economic goals
options.C: Family-oriented non-economic goals
options.D: Non-family oriented non-economic goals

questions.explanation: Firm growth and performance are non-family-oriented economic goals.

questions.question_text: When two brothers with equal ownership stakes in a family firm disagree over strategic direction, which type of agency cost does this conflict primarily represent?

options.A: Primary agency cost between principal and agent
options.B: Secondary agency cost between two principals
options.C: Transaction cost from asset specificity
options.D: Entrenchment cost from minority expropriation

questions.explanation: Conflict between two owners (principals) is a secondary, principal–principal agency cost.

questions.question_text: A technology startup founded by two siblings three years ago has not clarified whether they intend to pass the business to the next generation. Based on standard criteria for classifying family businesses, how should this company currently be classified?

options.A: Not a family business because it has two owners
options.B: A family business because it is unlisted
options.C: A family business because two related founders own it
options.D: Not a family business until intent to succession is evident

questions.explanation: Without evident intent to pass it on to the next generation (like Zerodha today), the firm is not yet a family business.

questions.question_text: Applying systems theory to a family business, why is the family subsystem typically described as more closed while the business subsystem is described as more open?

options.A: The family always ignores external events while the business always ignores emotions
options.B: The business has no interaction with suppliers or customers at all
options.C: The business must interact with markets while the family is driven by internal emotional dynamics
options.D: The family subsystem is legally required to disclose all information publicly

questions.explanation: The business must interact with markets (open), while the family runs on internal emotional dynamics (more closed).

questions.question_text: Under transaction cost economics applied to family businesses, reputation, tacit knowledge, and bonding or bridging social capital are best classified as which type of asset?

options.A: Generic tradable assets available across any firm
options.B: Generic non-tradable assets unique to the family business
options.C: Highly specific assets tied to a single machine
options.D: Publicly disclosed intangible assets under SEBI norms

questions.explanation: Reputation, tacit knowledge and social capital are generic non-tradable assets that can't easily move across firms.

questions.question_text: During severe economic crises, family firms typically exhibit greater financial resilience than non-family firms. Which strategic behavior primarily drives this resilience?

options.A: Maintaining conservative capital expenditure and leveraging established lender relationships
options.B: Aggressively acquiring distressed competitors and expanding into new markets
options.C: Increasing short-term debt financing to fund high-risk projects
options.D: Divesting core operating assets to maximize immediate cash reserves

questions.explanation: Family firms weather crises through conservative capex and long-standing lender and supplier relationships.

questions.question_text: Which three characteristics together determine whether a business qualifies as a family business?

options.A: Revenue, employee count, and market share
options.B: Listing status, brand name, and founder age
options.C: Ownership, management, and intent to succession
options.D: Capital structure, industry type, and location

questions.explanation: A family business is defined by ownership, management and intent to succession.

questions.question_text: What is the most commonly used criterion for classifying a business as a 'family business'?

options.A: Company is listed on a stock exchange
options.B: Business operates only in domestic markets
options.C: Significant family ownership and involvement in management
options.D: Business employs more than 100 people

questions.explanation: The common criterion is significant family ownership together with involvement in management.

questions.question_text: What is a 'family constitution' in the context of family business governance?

options.A: A written document outlining shared values, policies, and rules guiding the family's relationship with the business
options.B: A legal contract required for company incorporation
options.C: A financial statement summarizing family wealth
options.D: A marketing document describing the family brand

questions.explanation: A family constitution is a written document of shared values, policies and rules governing the family's relationship with the business.

questions.question_text:
An owner defines success not merely as maximising financial returns but as preserving the family name, maintaining long-term relationships and ensuring continuity across generations.
Which owner right is most directly reflected in this decision?

options.A: Right to decide
options.B: Right to value
options.C: Right to design
options.D: Right to transfer

questions.explanation: Defining success to include legacy, relationships and continuity reflects the owner's right to value.

questions.question_text:
Two siblings inherit a business equally. However, one sibling has expertise in operations and the other in finance. Both technically have equal ownership, but they divide management responsibilities according to their capabilities.
What does this arrangement illustrate?

options.A: Non-family employees are legally barred from promotions
options.B: Family members may be prioritized for leadership positions regardless of merit
options.C: Family firms cannot hire non-family employees
options.D: Non-family employees receive lower base salaries by law

questions.explanation: The only plausible option; the others describe legal rules that don't exist. (The options don't closely match the stem.)

questions.question_text:
Please Note: Questions 5–7 are based on the case provided below. Read the case carefully before attempting these questions.
Mehta Foods, a third-generation family enterprise, built its reputation on preserving traditional recipes and the family name across decades. When a large multinational offered to acquire the company at a substantial premium, the family patriarch declined, stating that selling would erase the identity his grandfather had created. His daughter, who manages finance, argued that the offer would secure the family's wealth and reduce financial risk, especially since the firm's core market was shrinking. Meanwhile, the patriarch's nephew, a shareholder uninvolved in operations, supported the sale, wanting liquidity to pursue his own ventures. Tensions grew as family members weighed emotional attachment against financial logic. The firm had no formal charter guiding such decisions, and disagreements were resolved informally around the dinner table, raising concerns about how future, larger disputes might be managed as the family and its shareholding base continued to expand.
questions.explanation: Shared passage for the questions that follow.

questions.question_text: What concept best explains the patriarch's reluctance to sell the business despite a lucrative offer?

options.A: Socioemotional wealth
options.B: Agency cost minimisation
options.C: Shareholder value maximisation
options.D: Portfolio diversification

questions.explanation: Valuing identity and legacy over a lucrative financial offer is socioemotional wealth.

questions.question_text: What underlying governance weakness does the absence of a formal charter reveal in Mehta Foods?

options.A: Lack of external customers for the firm's products
options.B: Lack of agreed rules for resolving major family-business decisions
options.C: Lack of any family members willing to work in the business
options.D: Lack of any ownership stake held by the family

questions.explanation: Without a formal charter, there are no agreed rules for resolving major family-business decisions.

questions.question_text: Which factor is most likely to intensify governance conflicts as Mehta Foods moves toward a cousin consortium structure?

options.A: Increased involvement of the founder in daily operations
options.B: A reduction in the total number of family shareholders
options.C: Divergent financial needs and interests among expanding family branches
options.D: Simplification of the firm's product portfolio

questions.explanation: As branches multiply in a cousin consortium, their differing financial needs and interests drive conflict.

questions.question_text:
A founder has created a highly successful business but refuses to delegate authority, develop contingency plans or prepare for succession. Almost every major decision depends on the founder.
Which combination of risks is most evident?

options.A: Low family involvement and excessive professionalisation
options.B: Excessive dependence on one individual and unclear succession
options.C: Excessive ownership dispersion and weak family identity
options.D: Strong governance and limited entrepreneurial control

questions.explanation: Everything depends on one person, with no delegation or succession plan.

questions.question_text:
A founder has the authority to determine the company's direction, choose its strategy and make major decisions without requiring approval from others. However, the same concentration of power creates significant dependence on the founder.
Which two ideas from the module best capture this situation?

options.A: Power to destroy and power to create
options.B: Power to create and power to sustain
options.C: Power to sustain and right to inform
options.D: Right to value and right to transfer

questions.explanation: The founder's authority reflects the power to create; the concentrated dependence also carries the power to destroy.

questions.question_text:
A large fourth-generation family business has multiple companies, with different family members responsible for different businesses. It has a family council and a written family constitution specifying who can join the business and what qualifications are required
What does this situation indicate?

options.A: The business is moving towards a controlling-owner model
options.B: Informal family relationships are sufficient for governance
options.C: The business has adopted a purely business-first philosophy
options.D: The family has developed more formal governance mechanisms appropriate to a family federation

questions.explanation: A family council and written constitution are formal governance mechanisms suited to a family federation.

questions.question_text: A founder observes fading interest among the children, a weakening competitive position, and a highly attractive acquisition offer. Which transfer pathway best fits this situation?

options.A: Divide the business among next-gen members
options.B: Sell the business to an outside buyer
options.C: Transfer the entire business to next-gen
options.D: Launch a new venture in the family galaxy

questions.explanation: Low next-gen interest, a weakening position and an attractive offer point to selling to an outside buyer.

questions.question_text: Which basis of successor commitment is characterized by a felt obligation to the family, often summarized by the phrase 'I ought to'?

options.A: Normative commitment
options.B: Affective commitment
options.C: Calculative commitment
options.D: Imperative commitment

questions.explanation: Normative commitment is a felt obligation to the family — 'I ought to'.

questions.question_text: A new leader discards proven practices wholesale and alienates long-serving veterans while pursuing rapid change. Which failure syndrome does this illustrate?

options.A: Conservative syndrome
options.B: Wavering syndrome
options.C: Rebellious syndrome
options.D: Circumstantial syndrome

questions.explanation: Discarding proven practices and alienating veterans in a rush to change is the rebellious syndrome.

questions.question_text: A family-firm heir completes an MBA, spends several years at a consulting firm and a multinational, then joins the family business through a clearly defined entry role. Which succession path does this describe?

options.A: Working outside, then returning
options.B: Bottom-up path within the firm
options.C: Job rotation across functions
options.D: New venture in family galaxy

questions.explanation: An MBA, outside work and then a defined entry role is the 'work outside, then return' path.

questions.question_text:
Read the following case let and answer the upcoming questions keep this in mind:-
Meera, the elder daughter of a manufacturing family, built a decade-long career at a global technology firm and is now a senior director there. Her father wants her to take over as CEO of the family business within two years. Meera has the analytical skill and leadership experience to run the firm, and colleagues at her current employer describe her as an outstanding operator. However, whenever the family raises the succession topic, she deflects the conversation, citing her fulfilling career and the autonomy she enjoys outside the family firm. She has never expressed genuine enthusiasm for the family business and seems to view any move into it as an obligation rather than a choice. Her father is considering announcing her as the designated successor at the next shareholder's meeting, believing her competence alone should settle the matter
questions.explanation: Shared passage for the questions that follow.

questions.question_text: Which quadrant of the Willingness–Ability matrix best describes Meera?

options.A: Ready Leader
options.B: Eager Apprentice
options.C: Reluctant Talent
options.D: Not (yet) a fit

questions.explanation: Meera is highly able but unwilling — a Reluctant Talent.

questions.question_text: What is the primary risk if Meera's father forces her into the CEO role despite her ambivalence?

options.A: Premature power before the incumbent can let go
options.B: Visible early failure due to sheltering an heir
options.C: Forced entry breeds disengagement and resentment
options.D: Soft accountability from running a pet project

questions.explanation: Forcing an unwilling successor in breeds disengagement and resentment.

questions.question_text: What is the recommended move for a successor who fits Meera's quadrant?

options.A: Build competence through outside roles and mentoring
options.B: Surface her motives and redesign the role for autonomy
options.C: Release her with dignity and appoint a non-family CEO
options.D: Stage authority through stretch assignments immediately

questions.explanation: For a reluctant talent, surface her motives and redesign the role to give her autonomy.

questions.question_text:
Read the following case let and answer the upcoming questions keep this in mind:-
Vikram has spent eighteen years chief financial officer of a family-owned retail chain and was widely seen as the second-in-command under the retiring founder. When the founder's son was named the new CEO instead, Vikram grew increasingly quiet in leadership meetings, stopped volunteering ideas, and began fielding calls from executive search firms. He confided to a colleague that he saw no clear path for his own growth under the new leadership and felt his decades of institutional knowledge were being overlooked. Within a few months, Vikram accepted an offer from a competitor, taking with him deep knowledge of supplier contracts and long-standing relationships with major retail partners that the family firm had relied on for years.
questions.explanation: Shared passage for the questions that follow.

questions.question_text: What move could the new CEO have taken to reduce the risk of losing Vikram?

options.A: Withhold information until trust is firmly established
options.B: Sequence change through pilots before scaling it
options.C: Create early proof points to convert sceptics
options.D: Retain by design through role clarity and incentives

questions.explanation: Retaining key non-family executives by design — clear roles and incentives — reduces the risk of losing them.

questions.question_text: Which stakeholder response category does Vikram's departure best represent?

options.A: Protect and mentor
options.B: Enable change
options.C: Wait and watch for failure
options.D: Leave the family firm

questions.explanation: Vikram's exit to a competitor is the 'leave the family firm' response.

questions.question_text: What is the main organisational risk illustrated by Vikram's exit?

options.A: The successor is cast as an insurgent leader
options.B: Knowledge and relationships walk out of the firm
options.C: An early stumble becomes a self-fulfilling story
options.D: The successor's promises remain untested by crisis

questions.explanation: His knowledge of supplier contracts and partner relationships walked out of the firm with him.

questions.question_text: In the three relationship systems framework used to analyse family firms, what currency does the business system primarily trade in?

options.A: Emotion: love and its opposites
options.B: Competence: knowledge and skill
options.C: Power: votes and voice
options.D: Status: title and seniority

questions.explanation: The family trades in emotion, the business in competence and skill, and ownership in power.

questions.question_text: In the tunneling and propping framework, what is the key distinguishing feature between the two forms of related-party value transfer?

options.A: Tunneling moves value to controllers while propping moves value into the firm
options.B: Tunneling always involves cash, while propping only involves shares
options.C: Propping harms minority shareholders while tunneling instead protects their interests
options.D: Tunneling occurs only during a crisis while propping occurs only in normal times

questions.explanation: Tunneling moves value out to controllers; propping moves value into the firm.

questions.question_text: A woman has real decision-making influence in a family firm but holds no title, does not appear on the organisation chart, and is consulted only privately. Which form of invisibility does this best illustrate?

options.A: Legal invisibility
options.B: Economic invisibility
options.C: Organisational invisibility
options.D: Narrative invisibility

questions.explanation: Real influence with no title or place on the org chart is organisational invisibility.

questions.question_text:
A family firm reports general satisfaction with its direction, makes timely decisions on critical issues with no unresolved tension left standing, and maintains relationships good enough to work and celebrate together, even though members do not always agree.
Using the three-question diagnostic for healthy conflict, how should this family's conflict level be assessed?

options.A: Too cold, because disagreements are being avoided beneath a surface of calm
options.B: In the Goldilocks zone, since all three conditions for healthy conflict are met
options.C: Inconclusive, because satisfaction with direction cannot be assessed without unanimous agreement
options.D: Too hot, because relationships show visible strain despite good decisions

questions.explanation: Satisfaction with direction, timely decisions and good relationships mean conflict is in the Goldilocks zone.

questions.question_text: A family decides that ownership shares will be split equally among all children, salaries will be based strictly on each child's role and performance, and a family fund will support any child facing genuine hardship. Which combination of distributive-justice rules does this reflect?

options.A: Equity for ownership, need for pay, equality for hardship support
options.B: Equality for ownership, equity for pay, need for hardship support
options.C: Need for ownership, equality for pay, equity for hardship support
options.D: Equality for ownership, need for pay, equity for hardship support

questions.explanation: Equal shares is equality, performance-based pay is equity, and the hardship fund is need.

questions.question_text: During an escalating family dispute, one branch hires a lawyer to represent its interests at a mediation session, and the opposing branch responds by hiring its own lawyer for the same meeting. According to Deutsch's description of how conflict intensifies, what best explains why this exchange is likely to deepen the dispute rather than resolve it?

options.A: Legal representation always eliminates emotional elements from a dispute
options.B: Hiring advocates automatically shifts the conflict from relationship to cognitive conflict
options.C: Competitive moves tend to invite competitive responses, tightening the spiral
options.D: Mediation sessions are only effective once lawyers are present on both sides

questions.explanation: Competitive moves invite competitive responses, tightening the conflict spiral.

questions.question_text: A family wants to apply the principle of 'fair process' to its decision about which relatives may enter the business, rather than announcing a rule unilaterally. Which sequence of actions best reflects the three principles of fair process in this domain?

options.A: Engage relatives in discussion, explain the reasoning, and set clear expectations for what follows
options.B: Announce the entry rule, survey employee satisfaction, and revisit it after five years
options.C: Consult only the founder, publish the decision, and discipline those who object
options.D: Benchmark competitor family firms, adopt their rule, and inform the family afterward

questions.explanation: Fair process means engaging people, explaining the reasoning and setting clear expectations.

questions.question_text:
Question 8-10 are based on the below mentioned case let. Please read the following case to attempt the questions.
Priya has worked unpaid in her family's textile business for over two decades, managing accounts, mediating disputes between her father and uncle, and training new employees, yet she holds no formal title, is absent from the organisational chart, and is not paid a salary. Her younger brother, with less experience, was recently named managing director and given a seat on the board. When Priya raised the issue of succession planning at a family gathering, her father dismissed her concerns, saying 'you have always been good with people, let your brother handle the business side.' Frustrated, Priya began quietly consulting a lawyer about her rights, while her brother felt increasingly cornered and stopped discussing company matters with her altogether. Their mother, who has mediated family disputes for years, fears that unless the family addresses these grievances directly and transparently, the growing silence between the two siblings could escalate into a more damaging confrontation.
questions.explanation: Shared passage for the questions that follow.

questions.question_text: Priya's two decades of unpaid, untitled work managing accounts and mediating disputes is best described using which concept from the study of women in family business?

options.A: The glass cliff
options.B: The mirrored ceiling
options.C: Organisational and economic invisibility
options.D: Primogeniture

questions.explanation: Unpaid, untitled work off the org chart is organisational and economic invisibility.

questions.question_text: Her father's comment that she is 'good with people' while her brother 'handles the business side' is an example of which risk associated with reported gender differences in working style?

options.A: Applying objective, written succession criteria fairly
options.B: Correcting for the mirrored ceiling through mentoring
options.C: Establishing a transparent ceiling through published policy
options.D: Using a perceived difference as an unjustified job filter

questions.explanation: Using a perceived gender difference ('good with people') to filter roles is unjustified.

questions.question_text: The siblings' current pattern of avoiding the topic entirely, even though both are privately frustrated, places their relationship at which stage of the family conflict spiral, and what does this suggest about the family's path forward?

options.A: Family war, suggesting litigation is now unavoidable
options.B: Advocates being called in, suggesting lawyers have already taken over
options.C: Communication breaking down, suggesting a need for ground rules before escalation
options.D: Interests diverging, suggesting the conflict has only just begun

questions.explanation: Going silent while privately frustrated is the 'communication breaking down' stage; ground rules are needed before it escalates.

questions.question_text: What is the primary driver for family businesses to pursue professionalisation as they grow in size and complexity?

options.A: The desire to remove all family members from the business entirely
options.B: The need for formal systems and specialised expertise beyond family capacity
options.C: Government regulations mandating non-family ownership
options.D: Pressure from competitors to merge with larger firms

questions.explanation: Growth and complexity create a need for formal systems and specialised expertise beyond what the family can provide.

questions.question_text: A third-generation family firm drafts a formal document outlining family values, employment policies for family members, and dispute resolution mechanisms. What is this document called?

options.A: Shareholder agreement
options.B: Memorandum of association
options.C: Annual report
options.D: Family constitution

questions.explanation: A formal document of family values, employment policies and dispute mechanisms is a family constitution.

questions.question_text:
Read the following case let and answer the upcoming 3 questions keep this in mind:-
After the sudden illness of the founder-CEO of Raghavan Pharma, the family faced an urgent decision about leadership succession. The founder's daughter, trained as a scientist, had deep knowledge of the company's core research but limited experience in managing large-scale operations and finance. The board, which included two independent directors brought in during an earlier professionalisation drive, suggested appointing an experienced external COO to support the daughter during the transition, allowing her to focus on R&D while gradually building managerial capability. Some family members felt this was an admission that the family could not run the business independently, while others saw it as a prudent step to ensure business continuity and protect stakeholder interests during a vulnerable period. The independent directors emphasised that combining family leadership with professional support was a common and effective practice among growing family enterprises navigating unplanned leadership transitions.
questions.explanation: Shared passage for the questions that follow.

questions.question_text: What role did the independent directors play in Raghavan Pharma's succession situation?

options.A: They recommended appointing an external COO to support the new family leader
options.B: They demanded immediate sale of the company to outside investors
options.C: They insisted the daughter resign from all company roles
options.D: They proposed shutting down the research and development division

questions.explanation: The independent directors recommended an external COO to support the daughter.

questions.question_text: What was the primary concern of family members who opposed bringing in an external COO?

options.A: The external COO would demand majority ownership stakes
options.B: It implied the family could not manage the business independently
options.C: The external COO lacked any relevant industry experience
options.D: It would violate government pharmaceutical regulations

questions.explanation: Opponents felt it implied the family couldn't run the business independently.

questions.question_text: What professionalisation practice from an earlier stage proved valuable during this leadership transition?

options.A: The presence of independent directors on the board
options.B: The complete removal of family members from management
options.C: The sale of company shares on a public stock exchange
options.D: The relocation of company headquarters overseas

questions.explanation: Independent directors appointed during the earlier professionalisation drive proved valuable.

questions.question_text: How does a family council differ functionally from a board of directors in a family business?

options.A: The family council manages daily operations while the board handles only family disputes
options.B: The family council has legal authority over company finances while the board has none
options.C: The family council addresses family relationships and values while the board focuses on business strategy and oversight
options.D: The family council and board perform identical functions and are interchangeable

questions.explanation: The family council handles family relationships and values; the board handles business strategy and oversight.

questions.question_text: A founder is considering hiring a professional, non-family CFO because the business has grown too complex for in-house family expertise. Which professionalisation practice does this illustrate?

options.A: Establishing a family constitution
options.B: Conducting a formal succession ceremony
options.C: Diversifying into unrelated industries
options.D: Bringing in external talent for specialised functional roles

questions.explanation: Hiring a non-family CFO brings external talent into a specialised functional role.

questions.question_text: Family firms often exhibit patient capital, meaning they are willing to accept lower short-term returns in exchange for what benefit relevant to innovation?

options.A: Avoidance of all long-term capital commitments
options.B: Faster exit through quick asset liquidation
options.C: Longer investment horizons that support sustained research and development
options.D: Immediate quarterly profit maximisation for shareholders

questions.explanation: Patient capital means longer investment horizons that support sustained R&D.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a common barrier to innovation adoption observed in family-owned businesses?

options.A: Emotional attachment to existing products and resistance to changing established practices
options.B: Excessive willingness to take uncalculated financial risks
options.C: Overreliance on external venture capital funding
options.D: Mandatory annual rotation of all leadership positions

questions.explanation: Emotional attachment to existing products and resistance to change are common barriers.

questions.question_text: Trans-generational entrepreneurship in family businesses is best understood as:

options.A: The legal process of converting a sole proprietorship into a partnership
options.B: The capability of a family to create economic and social value across successive generations through continued entrepreneurial behaviour
options.C: The transfer of ownership shares equally among all generational heirs
options.D: The practice of each generation starting a completely unrelated new venture

questions.explanation: Trans-generational entrepreneurship is a family's capability to create value across generations through continued entrepreneurial behaviour.
